1030.title: Lorenzo Ruiz (28 September)
1030.hook: a husband and father from Manila who boarded a ship in trouble and died a martyr in Japan
1030.howItsDone: Saint Lorenzo Ruiz and his companions are remembered on 28 September; in the Philippines and among Filipino communities abroad the day is kept with Mass, processions and novenas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wenceslaus, the duke the carol made a king. Your line was good king. Same feast day today, a different saint.

A man in Manila with a wife, children, and a steady job at his parish church. Then, suddenly, an accusation of a crime, and the threat of arrest. He does what frightened people do: he gets on a ship. It's carrying missionaries, and he doesn't fully know where it's headed. It carries him toward Japan, where the faith he grew up in has been outlawed. He wasn't sailing toward martyrdom. He was running from trouble. Today, Lorenzo Ruiz.
screen: `A FAMILY MAN IN MANILA.` → `AN ACCUSATION, A SHIP.` → `BOUND FOR JAPAN.`

segments.voice: Lorenzo Ruiz was born in Manila to a Chinese father and a Filipina mother, tradition says, and grew up close to the Dominican friars at the church in Binondo. He had beautiful handwriting, so he worked there as a scribe, copying documents. He married, and he and his wife had children. An ordinary, faithful life. Then came the accusation. What it was, and whether there was anything to it, the accounts leave unclear. To escape it, he joined a group of Dominican missionaries sailing north. They landed on Okinawa, were arrested, and were taken to Nagasaki. What happened next is why he's remembered. Lorenzo was not a priest or a friar. He was a layman who had come by accident. The authorities pressed him, under torture, to renounce his faith, and offered his life in return. Words remembered from his trial say he was a Catholic and would gladly die for God, and that if he had many lives, he would offer them all. He did not renounce. He was put to death in Nagasaki with his companions. Jesus says in the gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Every one therefore that shall confess me before men, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven." Lorenzo made that confession far from home, among strangers. The Church canonized him with his companions, and Filipino Catholics honor him as the first saint of the Philippines: not a missionary hero, but a frightened father who, when it mattered, stood still.

segments.voice: Bring to mind the Philippines: crowded churches, families in Manila, and Filipinos working far from home as nurses, sailors and caregivers, by name if you know one. If you pray, ask Lorenzo Ruiz, a man who also ended up far from home, to pray for them; if you don't, simply send them your good will.

1031.title: Michael, Gabriel and Raphael (29 September)
1031.hook: three angels with names: the protector, the messenger and the healer
1031.howItsDone: The feast of Saints Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, archangels, is kept on 29 September; some Catholics pray the Saint Michael prayer, attributed to Pope Leo XIII, at home, and some parishes say it after Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lorenzo Ruiz, the scribe from Manila who would not deny his faith in Japan. Your line was first of the philippines.

Angels in the Bible often appear, speak and vanish without giving a name. When Jacob wrestles through the night with the one the prophet Osee later calls an angel, and asks its name, the answer is a question back: why do you ask? So when an angel in scripture does say its name, people pay attention. The Catholic calendar keeps one feast for three of them together: one who fights, one who announces, one who heals.
screen: `ANGELS WITHOUT NAMES.` → `THREE WHO HAVE THEM.` → `ONE FEAST FOR ALL THREE.`

segments.voice: The word is archangel: a chief angel, one with a particular task. Start with Michael. In the book of Daniel he's a great prince who stands for his people. In the Apocalypse, the book many call Revelation, Michael and his angels fight the dragon. Tradition reads his Hebrew name as a question: who is like God? A small scene in the letter of Jude shows what that question means. Michael, the archangel, is arguing with the devil over the body of Moses. He could hurl an insult. He doesn't. He says only, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord command thee." The warrior angel won't claim the fight as his own. Gabriel is the messenger. He comes to Zechariah in the Temple and to Mary in Nazareth, and when he's doubted, he introduces himself: "I am Gabriel, who stand before God." His job is to carry news, often news that seems impossible. Raphael is the healer and the traveling companion. His story is in the book of Tobias, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians count as scripture and Protestant churches generally do not. He walks beside young Tobias on a long journey, disguised as an ordinary man, and helps heal Tobias's blind father. Only at the end does he reveal himself: "I am the angel Raphael, one of the seven, who stand before the Lord." A protector, a messenger, a healer. And each one, in the end, points away from himself and toward God.
screen: `MICHAEL: WHO IS LIKE GOD?` · `THE LORD COMMAND THEE.` · `GABRIEL, WHO STANDS BEFORE GOD.` · `RAPHAEL, THE HEALER IN DISGUISE.` · then, large: `EACH POINTS PAST HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Some Catholics pray a short prayer to Saint Michael, asking him to defend us in the struggle with evil; if you pray, say it slowly now, or ask for protection in your own words, handing the fight to God the way Michael did. If you don't pray, bring to mind one battle you're in right now, notice how much of it you've been trying to win alone, and let it rest for a moment.

Your line: who is like god. A name that is a question. See you tomorrow.

1032.title: The Guardian Angels (2 October)
1032.hook: a knock at the gate, a servant girl, and a room that says: it is his angel
1032.howItsDone: The memorial of the Holy Guardian Angels is kept on 2 October; Catholic children are taught a short prayer to their guardian angel, the Angele Dei, to say in the morning and at night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the archangels: Michael, Gabriel and Raphael. Your line was who is like god.

Night in Jerusalem. A house full of people praying for Peter, who is in prison. Knocking at the outer gate. A servant girl named Rhoda goes to answer, hears Peter's voice, and is so overjoyed she runs back inside without opening the gate. Peter's out there, she tells them. They say she's mad. She insists. And then they say something strange, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is his angel." Meanwhile Peter keeps knocking. Today, the guardian angels.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE GATE.` → `RHODA FORGETS TO OPEN IT.` → `IT IS HIS ANGEL.`

segments.voice: That scene in Acts is funny, and it's also a window. When Rhoda insists Peter is at the gate, the believers' first guess isn't a ghost or a mistake. It's his angel. They took for granted that a person might have an angel of his own. Catholics build on that, and on a line from Jesus himself. In Matthew, he sets a child in front of the disciples and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "See that you despise not one of these little ones: for I say to you, that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven." Even the smallest, the ones adults overlook, have someone in God's presence on their behalf. Psalm ninety, in the Douay-Rheims numbering, says it as a promise: "For he hath given his angels charge over thee; to keep thee in all thy ways." From those threads comes the long Catholic tradition that each person has an angel, a guardian, given by God to watch over them through life. The Church keeps a feast for them on the second of October, a few days after the archangels. Notice what a guardian angel is not: not a pet spirit, not a lucky charm, not someone you become when you die. In Catholic teaching, angels are their own kind of creature. The guardian's job is quiet: to stay close, and to keep turning a person toward God. That's why the old children's prayer to the guardian angel asks it to light, guard, rule and guide. Not to perform. To stay beside.
screen: `THE BELIEVERS GUESS: IT IS HIS ANGEL.` · `THEIR ANGELS SEE THE FACE OF MY FATHER.` · `HIS ANGELS CHARGE OVER THEE.` · `NOT A CHARM: A COMPANION AT YOUR SIDE.` · then, large: `TO KEEP THEE IN ALL THY WAYS.`

segments.voice: Think back over a stretch of your life and notice one moment when something kept you: a near miss, the right person at the right time, a voice in your head that said wait. If you pray, thank your guardian angel for that moment, plainly, the way a child might; if you don't, just notice that you were kept, and give thanks, if you like, to whoever or whatever was beside you.
Messenger, what the Greek word angel means. In Catholic teaching, the guardian angel God gives each person stays close and keeps turning them toward God.

1033.title: Bruno (6 October)
1033.hook: a famous teacher walks away into the mountains and founds an order of silence
1033.carry: the cross stands while the world turns
1033.howItsDone: Saint Bruno is remembered on 6 October; Carthusian monks and nuns keep it as their founder's feast inside their charterhouses, which the public generally does not visit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guardian angels, and Rhoda leaving Peter at the gate. Your line was beside you.

A man at the top of his field. He runs a cathedral school, his students go on to high office, and one of them will one day become pope. People expect him to rise. Instead, he and a few companions walk up into the mountains above Grenoble, into a wild valley, and build huts. No lecture hall, no audience, almost no talking. Just prayer and work and silence. The place gave its name to a way of life. Today's word is that name.
screen: `A TEACHER AT THE TOP.` → `UP INTO THE MOUNTAINS.` → `A VALLEY OF SILENCE.`

segments.voice: The word is Carthusian. It names the monks and nuns who follow the way Saint Bruno began in those mountains, called the Chartreuse. Bruno had been a respected teacher at Reims, in France. Tradition says he grew sick of the politics and money around him and wanted God alone. The local bishop, Hugh, gave him and his companions the land, and they built a hermitage there: the Grande Chartreuse. Here's how a Carthusian lives, then and now. Each monk has his own cell, really a small house with a garden and a workshop. He prays, reads, works and eats there, mostly alone. The monks come together in church for the long night prayers and for Mass, and on certain days they share a meal and a walk. Silence runs through the whole day: not as a punishment, but as room to listen. The Douay-Rheims gives a psalm line they could take as a rule: "Be still and see that I am God." Bruno himself didn't get to stay. His old student became Pope Urban the Second and called him to Rome as an adviser. Bruno went, obeyed, and then asked to leave. He founded another hermitage in Calabria, in southern Italy, and died there. The Carthusians' motto, in Latin, is Stat crux dum volvitur orbis: the cross stands while the world turns. Bruno himself never lived in that valley again. Up in the cells he left behind, the same prayer went on.
screen: `BRUNO LEAVES A BRILLIANT CAREER.` · `A CELL, A GARDEN, A WORKSHOP.` · `BE STILL AND SEE THAT I AM GOD.` · `THE CROSS STANDS WHILE THE WORLD TURNS.` · then, large: `STAT CRUX DUM VOLVITUR ORBIS.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes, no words at all, not even in your head if you can manage it; when a sentence starts forming, let it go unfinished, and notice how much of your mind is talk. If you pray, hold the psalm line, be still, and let the rest fall quiet; if you don't, simply rest in the quiet.

1034.title: Denis (9 October)
1034.hook: a stone bishop in Paris holds his own head in his hands
1034.howItsDone: Saint Denis and companions are remembered on 9 October; in France, and especially in Paris and at the basilica of Saint-Denis north of the city, the feast is kept with Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bruno, and the Carthusians in their silent valley. Your line was the cross stands while the world turns.
screen: `THE CROSS STANDS WHILE THE WORLD TURNS.`

segments.voice: On the front of Notre-Dame in Paris, among the carved saints, stands a bishop in his robes. Where his head should be, there's nothing. His head is in his hands, held out in front of him, still wearing its miter. Tourists photograph him and wonder. Parisians have a story ready, and it starts on a hill at the edge of their city, where the white church of Sacré-Cœur stands now. Today, Denis.
screen: `A STONE BISHOP AT NOTRE-DAME.` → `HIS HEAD IN HIS HANDS.` → `A HILL AT THE EDGE OF PARIS.`

segments.voice: Start with an early layer of the story, from Gregory of Tours, a bishop who wrote a history of the Franks. He says Denis was sent to Gaul, to the town that would become Paris, as its bishop, and that he died by the sword for Christ. Other old accounts fill in more: he preached, people came to faith, and in a time of persecution he was arrested with two companions, a priest named Rusticus and a deacon named Eleutherius, and all three were beheaded. That's the core the Church keeps on his feast: Denis and companions, martyrs. Then the legend grew. Later tellings say that after Denis was beheaded on the hill, he stood up, picked up his own head, and walked away, preaching as he went, until he reached the place where he wanted to be buried. That's the bishop on the front of Notre-Dame. It's a story people tell, not a record. Some read it as a picture of how Parisians felt: their bishop was not finished by a sword. And the hill? Tradition reads its name, Montmartre, as the mountain of martyrs. Historians debate where the name really comes from, but the story stuck to the place. One more twist. In Acts, when Paul preaches in Athens, among those who believe is a man named Dionysius the Areopagite. Medieval writers decided that Dionysius and Denis were the same man, Paul's convert sailing to Paris. Today the Church treats them as two different saints: same name, different men, mixed together by people who loved them both.
screen: `SENT TO GAUL AS BISHOP.` · `BEHEADED WITH HIS TWO COMPANIONS.` · `THE LEGEND: HE CARRIED HIS HEAD.` · `NOT THE MAN PAUL MET IN ATHENS.` · then, large: `MONTMARTRE: THE MOUNTAIN OF MARTYRS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind France: Paris and its old churches, small villages with a bell tower in the center, and people of every faith and none who live there now, starting with anyone French you know. If you pray, ask Denis, the bishop on the hill, to pray for the country he served; if you don't, simply hold its people in mind with good will.

Your line: the mountain of martyrs. A legend grew, and the hill kept the name. One thousand thirty-four days now.

1035.title: Callistus (14 October)
1035.hook: a slave who lost his master's money, worked the mines, and became bishop of Rome
1035.howItsDone: Pope Saint Callistus I is remembered on 14 October; in Rome, pilgrims visit the Catacombs of Saint Callistus on the Appian Way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Denis, and the hill of Montmartre. Your line was the mountain of martyrs.

A slave in Rome is trusted with his master's money. He runs a kind of bank, and other Christians deposit their savings with him. Then the money is gone. He panics and runs. He's caught, punished, and later sent to labor in the mines of Sardinia. On any list of future popes, his name would not appear. And yet some years later, the man from the mines is bishop of Rome. Today, Callistus.
screen: `A SLAVE WITH A BANK.` → `THE MONEY IS GONE.` → `FROM THE MINES TO ROME.`

segments.voice: Much of what we know about Callistus comes from someone who disliked him: Hippolytus, a Roman priest and writer who opposed him bitterly. So read the story with that in mind. The bank failure, the flight, the mines: Hippolytus tells it to make Callistus look bad. Some readers today come away liking Callistus more. Released from Sardinia, he lived quietly outside Rome for a time; later the bishop of Rome, Zephyrinus, took him in, made him a deacon, and put him in charge of the Christian burial ground on the Appian Way. Those underground galleries still bear his name: the Catacombs of Saint Callistus. Then he was chosen bishop of Rome himself. Here's what made Hippolytus so angry. Callistus allowed Christians who had committed serious sins, and had done penance, to be welcomed back to communion. Hippolytus thought that was far too soft. Cornelius would face the same question after him. Some readers see Callistus's own story in his answer: a man who had failed with other people's money, been punished, and been given a second chance, now keeping the door open for others. In Matthew, Peter asks Jesus how often he must forgive. Seven times? The answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "I say not to thee, till seven times; but till seventy times seven times." Tradition says Callistus died a martyr. And tradition says Hippolytus, in time, was reconciled to the Church and also died a martyr. The Church now honors them both as saints. The angry critic and the forgiving shepherd ended up on the same calendar.
screen: `HIS STORY COMES FROM A RIVAL.` · `KEEPER OF THE CATACOMBS.` · `HE WELCOMED BACK THOSE WHO REPENTED.` · `BOTH MEN BECAME SAINTS.` · then, large: `SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN TIMES.`

segments.voice: Think of a person who let you or others down and has tried to make it right, and notice whether there's a door in you still shut against them. You don't have to fling it open; just see if it could open a crack. If you pray, bring them before God by name; if you don't, simply picture greeting them warmly, once.
Callistus. A slave who failed, was punished, came back, kept the catacombs, and as bishop of Rome welcomed back sinners who repented.
Your line: from slave to shepherd. A second chance, passed on to others. See you tomorrow.

1036.title: Hedwig (16 October)
1036.hook: a duchess walks barefoot through the snow, carrying the shoes she was told to wear
1036.howItsDone: Saint Hedwig is remembered on 16 October; she is honored in Poland and Germany, and Catholics in Silesia, especially at Trzebnica where she is buried, keep her feast with Mass and pilgrimage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Callistus, the slave who became bishop of Rome and welcomed sinners back. Your line was from slave to shepherd.

Winter in Silesia. A duchess is walking to church barefoot, on frozen ground, as she does to share a little of what the poor feel. Her confessor, worried, orders her to wear shoes. She obeys. She carries them. That's the story people tell, half a joke and half a portrait: a woman who did what she was told, and still found a way to stand where the poor stood. Today, Hedwig.
screen: `BAREFOOT ON FROZEN GROUND.` → `TOLD TO WEAR SHOES.` → `SHE CARRIES THEM.`

segments.voice: Hedwig was born into a noble family in Bavaria and married Henry, who became duke of Silesia, a land now mostly in Poland. German by birth and Silesian by marriage, she is honored today by both Germans and Poles. In Polish, she's Jadwiga. She had wealth and power, and she spent a great deal of both on others. With her husband she founded a convent at Trzebnica for Cistercian nuns, and she supported hospitals and fed the poor, tradition says, sometimes serving them at her own table. Her life was not easy. She outlived her husband and some of her children. Her son Henry was killed in battle defending the land against invaders. In her last years Hedwig lived at the convent she had founded, among the nuns, and she died there. What made her giving different? It wasn't only large gifts from a distance. It was close: walking where the poor walked, eating with them, using her rank to open doors for them. Paul has a line about that kind of giving, in the Douay-Rheims: "For God loveth a cheerful giver." The Greek word behind cheerful there is hilaros: glad. A glad heart, not a grim duty. And it doesn't take a duchy. In the same verse Paul says each one should give as he has decided in his heart, and a chapter earlier he says a gift is measured by what a person has, not by what he hasn't. Hedwig had a great deal and gave it gladly. The same gladness fits a smaller purse.
screen: `GERMAN BY BIRTH, SILESIAN BY MARRIAGE.` · `A CONVENT, HOSPITALS, BREAD FOR THE POOR.` · `LAST YEARS IN THE CONVENT SHE FOUNDED.` · `GOD LOVETH A CHEERFUL GIVER.` · then, large: `OUT OF WHAT YOU HAVE.`

segments.voice: Take a quiet inventory, not only your money but your time this week, a skill, a coat you don't wear, a meal you could share, and let one thing you could actually give rise to the top. Notice whether the thought of giving it feels glad or grim. If you pray, offer it to God and ask for a cheerful heart; if you don't, simply let the glad part grow.
Hedwig. Jadwiga in Polish. A duchess of Silesia who founded a convent, fed the poor, walked where they walked, and gave gladly.
Your line: the duchess who gave. She gave gladly, out of what she had. That's day one thousand thirty-six.
